30-second read The whole story in STAR
S · Situation

Production, safety, environmental and royalty data lived in 7 hand-kept spreadsheets. Acting on a gas alert took 4.2 minutes, and staff were unsure where digital tools left their jobs.

T · Task

Project design lead for 18 weeks, not a line manager. Directed 3 designers, working with a PM, architect, data scientist and 4 engineers.

A · Action

Killed the alert-first concept · moved 3D to Phase 2 · AI recommends, a person confirms.

R · Result

In simulated testing (n=8): 84 s to decide vs 4.2 min on Excel (−67%), 89% task completion. A 4-week pilot with 3 supervisors was reported; its usage was not documented.

Next

Test whether triage misses any critical alert on replayed shifts (target: none missed), then a 3-site rollout with Excel running in parallel.

S1 · Problem statement Lean UX canvas

Mining ran on lagging, siloed data, and the workforce was unsure where it fit.

The problem

Traditional mining operations suffer from inefficient resource use, safety risks, environmental concerns and no real-time decision-making. Meanwhile, the workforce faces uncertainty from technological disruption.

How might we create a digital platform that improves operational efficiency, safety and sustainability, while supporting workforce transformation through upskilling and evolving job roles?
Value proposition Tap a pillar to trace it

Real-time monitoring, predictive analytics and automation of manual and hazardous tasks, built on centralised data, so operations improve and people gain new digital skills and roles.

S2 · Today's workflow Manual Excel workflow

Seven spreadsheets and a phone tree stood between a reading and a decision.

Every shift, people read gauges and devices, typed the values into shared Excel files, then phoned each other to check them. Data arrived hours late, in several copies, with typing errors.

Time to decide · once the alert is seen
4:12

minutes from seeing the alert to choosing an action, in a simulated test. Finding out about the hazard takes longer.

Find sheet & row 1.1 mCall to verify 1.4 mRadio for crew 1.2 mDecide 0.5 m

Split modelled from shift shadowing · total measured

Two clocks, not one Real response time = time to find out + time to decide

In the real Excel workflow, acting on a hazard takes far longer than 4.2 minutes.

4.2 min was measured in a simulated test that showed participants the alert straight away. On site, nobody sees a hazard until it has been radioed in or typed into a sheet. That wait comes first, and it was not part of the test.

Radioed straight inUrgent hazard, e.g. a gas alarm called in
≈ 9 min
Waits for the spreadsheetRoutine reading that later turns out to matter
≈ 2.5 h
Find out · modelled from shadowing (≈5 min radio relay; or ≈2 h average batch wait + 25 min to share and check)Decide · measured 4.2 min

Why 4.2 is still the headline comparison: it is the only part measured on both workflows, so 4.2 min → 84 s compares like with like. SMMS is designed to shrink the first clock too (sensor streaming, seconds instead of hours), but that part is modelled, not tested. Worth confirming with the client whether their “> 4 min” response-time goal meant the decision step or the whole chain.

Disclaimer · where this data comes from

UX research: the tile figures (23 crew, 68 gas alerts, 12 machines, 2.8k t target) and the spreadsheet workflow describe one typical 8-hour shift, observed through shift shadowing at 3 mine sites and 14 interview sessions. Usability testing: the workload scores come from moderated sessions with 8 participants per round in simulated incidents, scored with NASA-TLX after each session: 74 at the baseline (concept-stage) session and 31 in usability round 2. Time and error figures for the spreadsheet workflow are modelled estimates, not live measurements.

T1 · Mandate What I was brought in to do

Lead the UX from zero: no design system, no patterns, no prior research.

The engineering team had a data pipeline but no product surface. I was the project design lead for 18 weeks, directing 2 product designers and 1 junior designer. I was not their line manager.

Goals from the client brief Brief
  1. Respond fasterCut average incident response from over 4 minutes to under 90 seconds.
  2. One surfaceReplace disconnected tools (today: 7 spreadsheets, phone and radio) with one operational view.
  3. Automate complianceOfficers spent 40% of each shift on manual regulatory reporting.
  4. See failures earlyPredictive maintenance visibility across 294 licensed mine sites.
  5. National viewA real-time production dashboard for client leadership.

  • 18 weeksResearch to pilot-ready build.
  • AI latencyCloud inference took 6–9 s over cellular, too slow for triage.
  • Incomplete 3D dataSurvey data was missing for 60% of sites.
  • Human sign-offThe client's legal team required a named person to approve every action.
  • ConnectivityUnderground links drop; the product had to say what happens offline.
  • Site accessPermits limited in-person research to 3 of 14 sessions.

A1 · Three consequential calls What was at stake, who pushed back, what it cost

Three decisions shaped everything that followed. The evidence for each is below.

1

Kill the alert-first concept

Week 7
At stake
Three weeks of concept work, and the concept operations liked because it looked like their control room.
Pushback
Operations leads, whose mental model was "show every alert".
Trade-off
Rebuilt the core layout mid-project, inside the 18-week plan.
Outcome
Decision time on the canvas prototype: 3.4 min in round 1, 84 s in round 2, against 4.2 min on the Excel workflow. (The paper concept test is not comparable.)
2

Move the 3D digital twin to Phase 2

Concept phase
At stake
The brief asked for a full 3D twin. It would have been the showpiece of the client demo.
Pushback
The brief and client expectations.
Trade-off
Less visual impact in the demo, in exchange for something usable under pressure.
Outcome
Survey data was incomplete for 60% of sites, and the 2D canvas tested easier to read.
3

AI recommends, a person confirms

Architecture
At stake
Fully automatic escalation would look faster on paper.
Pushback
The brief asked for AI that could escalate and dispatch on its own.
Trade-off
One confirm tap per action.
Outcome
Met the client's legal rule, created a named audit trail, and became the AI principles.

A3 · The turn Critical finding

Once an alert fires, supervisors look for Where → Who before severity. The spreadsheets put location last.

How supervisors triage
1st
Where?
exact zone
2nd
Who?
crew in that zone
3rd
What next?
severity, cause & action
How the spreadsheets answered
1st
Severity
a hand-typed column

Category
one workbook per type
3rd
Location
free-text cell, often blank
What Rajesh said Interview quoteI need to know what's wrong, where it is, and who's near it — in that order.

“What's wrong” here is the alert type, such as gas. The spreadsheet row already shows that.

What we saw Observed · n=6Where exactly? → Who is in that zone? → What happened and what action is needed?

Asked before severity, cause or recommended action. Both accounts put place and people ahead of the detail the sheets lead with.

This mismatch is the most likely contributor to the 4.2-minute delay, and it is why the product starts from a spatial canvas instead of an alert list.

Testing did not isolate information order from navigation, data freshness or context integration. The 84 s result reflects all four changes together.

A5 · Alignment Operations, safety, engineering

Three teams wanted three things. One role-adaptive model gave each its lens.

Operations wanted
“Show everything, all the time.”
National overview with one-click drill-down to any mine.
Safety wanted
“Fewer things asking for attention.”
AI triage rules: 240 logged events → 18 surfaced, compliance items first.
Engineering worried
“Offline sync is complex and risky.”
Proposed priority-queue sync: safety data first, analytics later.
Same data · three lenses · resolved in 2 workshops
1One problem statement

"Supervisors need location and people before severity." Signed off by operations, safety and engineering in the 2 alignment workshops after the concept review.

2Role-lens ranking

Each team ranked its top 3 information needs. The rankings showed three different first screens on one data model.

3Demo the drill-down

Operations saw any mine one click from the national view: "everything, one click away" instead of "everything on one screen".

✕What I said no to

One screen with every sensor · three separate apps · full offline sync for analytics in phase 1.

One disagreement in detail Operations vs safety, at the concept review
Competing needs

Operations wanted every site and sensor visible at once. Safety wanted fewer things asking for attention.

Evidence I used

58% of alerts dismissed unread by hour 4 (n=8) · the alert-first concept reproduced that fatigue in testing · supervisors looked for place and people first (n=6).

Concessions

Operations kept a national overview, one click from any mine. Safety got triage instead of a full feed. Engineering got safety-first sync, with no analytics offline in phase 1.

Final decision

One data model with role-adaptive views, agreed in 2 workshops.

Consequence

A 2-week delay, absorbed inside the 18 weeks. In hindsight I aligned the teams too late; next time this happens before research synthesis.

A6 · AI triage Intelligence layer

240 logged events in, 18 surfaced items out.

Today, each of these readings is typed into a spreadsheet by hand. SMMS is designed to ingest them directly and surface only what needs a person, with a confidence score, a one-line reason and a recommended action.

Event · 240

One line in the shift logs: a sensor reading out of range, an equipment warning, a compliance flag or a repeat. Average of 3 audited shifts (720 in total).

Duplicate · 62

The same sensor reporting the same condition again. Merged into one item; the repeats stay in the log.

Alert

An event that asks a person to look. Today every event is treated as one, which is why 58% were dismissed unread by hour 4.

Surfaced item · 18

Shown to a role with a reason, a confidence score and a suggested action. The other 222 are kept and visible on demand, not deleted.

What 240 → 18 does and does not show

The figure comes from applying the triage rules to 3 logged shifts, not from a live model. Nobody has yet checked whether any of the 222 events not surfaced was a real hazard, so it shows less noise for the user, not accuracy. Recall and precision are tested in the AI evaluation plan (section 11).

Safety-critical items surfaced fell from 72 to 8.

Per-shift events by category · before vs after triage rules · the 64 safety events not surfaced were merged or set to monitor; none has been checked against what actually happened

AI recommends. A named human decides.

AI can
  • Rank and de-duplicate alerts
  • Predict failures 4–72 h ahead (target, unvalidated)
  • Explain why an item is critical
  • Forecast ore with a confidence range
AI cannot
  • Act on an alert by itself
  • Dispatch teams or evacuate
  • Show advice without its confidence
  • Log an action with no human approver

Reported three-shift log audit. Fewer alerts does not prove accuracy: critical-alert recall needs the replay test before any site relies on triage.

A9 · Product surfaces Concept surfaces

Six surfaces share one map and one visual language.

The 10 wireframe screens were consolidated into 6 product surfaces. Each is mapped back to the problems found in research, the design decisions that address them, and the impact so far.

Tap a numbered marker to see the design decision behind that part of the screen. Tap the image for full size.

Research and testing took place in underground mines. These screens apply the visual direction to an open-pit site and were not the interface tested. What transfers: the spatial canvas, alerts pinned in place with people nearby, role lenses and stale-data labels. What likely needs adapting: GPS for vehicles instead of UWB and RFID tags, much larger zones, and dust and glare instead of low light. Not yet tested in an open-pit setting. Third-party logos are blurred and dashboard values are illustrative.

  • Data migration12 months of gas, incident and maintenance logs imported for trends and audits.
  • Role-based training90-minute sessions per role plus in-app first-run tips; supervisors first.
  • People impactShift clerks move from typing readings to data-quality checks: sensor faults, missing tags.
  • ChampionsOne supervisor per shift as the go-to person for questions and feedback.

A11 · How I led Rhythm, quality bar, coaching, handoff

I set the quality bar and made the hard calls, so three designers could move fast.

Weekly rhythm Every ritual ends in a decision
  1. Mon
    Brief and priorities · 30 min

    One problem per designer, with success criteria written before any pixels.

  2. Wed
    Design crit · 60 min

    Feedback against the shared criteria: observation, then reason, then recommendation.

  3. Fri
    Decision review with PM and architect

    Each review ends with a logged decision or one named open question.

  4. 2 wks
    Field check

    A flow tested with supervisors, remote or on site, before it moves to hi-fi.

Coaching, not designing Junior designer → compliance owner

Challenge: moving from producing wireframes to owning decisions on a regulated flow, where a missing field becomes an audit gap.

Wk 1–4

Paired on wireframes; I set the brief and reviewed daily.

Wk 5–8

They presented in Wednesday crit, with me as backup.

Wk 9–12

Owned the compliance flow end to end; I moved to review only.

Observable change: by week 12 they led the compliance screen independently and presented its trade-offs in crit themselves, which freed me for client workshops. Reported

R1 · Measured results Simulated testing · reported pilot

In simulated testing, deciding on a critical alert fell from 4.2 minutes to 84 seconds.

Critical alert · time to decision
84s

down 67% from 4.2 minutes on the Excel + radio workflow

How it's calculated
Excel + radio252 s
SMMS, round 284 s
4.2 min × 60 = 252 s
252 s − 84 s = 168 s saved
168 ÷ 252 = 0.667 → 67% less time

Decision step only. Time to find out about a hazard (≈9 min to ≈2.5 h on Excel, modelled) is not included in either number. Stopwatch timing from the moment a critical alert appeared to the moment the participant confirmed an action, averaged across 7 simulated incident scenarios with 8 participants. The baseline ran the same scenarios on the spreadsheet, phone and radio workflow, in counterbalanced order; raw timings were not supplied.

Formula: (entry time × 240 − 18 × 10 s) × 3 shifts × days × adoption, plus (3.2 h − report time) × 3 × days × adoption. Not netted out: new duties (weekly review of 50 suppressed items, sensor data-quality checks) and possible overlap if officers' reporting time includes copying the same readings clerks type. The low case absorbs some of this by keeping 1.0 h of reporting. Implementation cost (sensors, tags, edge gateways, integration, training) was not available, so no ROI or payback is claimed.

Model assumptions
  • 240 readings and events per shift, from the three-shift log audit; today each is typed by hand.
  • 45 seconds per manual entry (find the file, locate the row, type, save); 10 seconds per SMMS confirmation.
  • Shared sheets updated in batches about every 4 hours, so data is about 2 hours old on average.
  • 3% manual entry error rate: an assumption within the commonly cited 1–4% range for hand-keyed data, not measured at the client. Only re-typing errors are counted.
  • 3 shifts a day, one safety officer per shift spending 40% of 8 hours on reporting (from research); 30 minutes to review an auto-generated report.
  • 5-second refresh and one-tap confirmation are proposed SMMS behaviours, not yet validated in live operations.
  • Hours are capacity that could be redirected, not cash savings: no staffing change was demonstrated.
How the testing worked
Participants

8 per round, recruited from 3 sites: 4 shift supervisors, 2 safety officers, 2 operations managers. Screened to exclude anyone involved in the brief. Whether round 2 used the same 8 people as round 1 is not documented.

Tasks

7 simulated scenarios: gas leak, equipment failure triage, crew location, compliance export, shift handover, maintenance scheduling, production review. Timed from alert visible to action confirmed.

Baseline and order

Within-subject: the same scenarios were run on the Excel, phone and radio workflow and on SMMS, in counterbalanced order. Raw timings and the exact order were not supplied.

Conditions

Round 1: Figma interactive prototype. Round 2: scenario-based test prototype. Simulated incidents, not live operations. Underground scenarios.

Comparability

Rounds 1 and 2 share cohort size, tasks and instruments. The concept test does not: paper prototypes, 4 people per concept. It is shown for direction only.

Still needed

Task-level completed/attempted counts, partial-completion rules, NASA-TLX scoring method (raw or weighted), and the SUS cohort.

Guardrails Design requirements, to be verified Target
  • No critical alert hidden by a role filter. Verify: replay test, recall of critical events.
  • Model confidence does not lower the severity of a sensor reading. Verify: rule review and test cases.
  • Every action has a named human approver. Verify: audit-log check in the pilot.
  • If supervisors override more than 20% of suggestions in a week, the rules are reviewed.

Lessons this project supports, and what I would change next time.

Reflection What carries forward

Show location first, explain every AI call, and say what offline can't do.

LEARNING 01

Spatial context supports triage

Location and affected people belong together. Maps are not better for every task, so keep an alert-first fallback to test.

LEARNING 02

AI needs visible evidence

Users distrusted unexplained priorities. Show the reason and confidence, and keep human approval.

LEARNING 03

Offline needs explicit limits

Stale data, pending sync and unavailable info must be shown per role, not hidden.

Next time What I'd change

More time on site

Only 3 of 14 sessions were in person, yet they revealed the shadow systems. I'd push for 8+.

Align stakeholders earlier

The ops-vs-safety conflict surfaced at concept review and cost 2 weeks. I'd run a shared problem workshop before synthesis.

Design for the cause

Concept C treated the symptom (alerts). The cause was missing spatial context.
